transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-08-29
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Sam Rivera (Redwood AE), Priya Natarajan (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Quantum Harbor CTO), Renee Martinez (Head of ML), Dev Patel (Infra)

Summary (auto): quick intake to map per-workflow cost, see if Hosted pilot meets latency/cost goals, and identify what Dedicated/Private would buy them.

[00:00] Sam Rivera: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Sam from Redwood, joined by Priya, our infra SE. Quick intros?
[00:12] Liam O'Connor: Liam here, CTO at Quantum Harbor, we run a customer-facing conversational triage flow, fairly high QPS at peak, um, roughly 20k queries/day currently in beta.
[00:23] Renee Martinez: Renee, head of ML, working on prompts and response ranking; our main concern is unit cost once we go to prod and keeping latency tight.
[00:33] Dev Patel: Dev, infra, I'll be owner for any VPC or private deployment work and collecting traffic patterns.
[00:38] Priya Natarajan: Hey all — Priya from Redwood, I focus on runtime and batching strategies.
[00:42] Sam Rivera: Cool. Objective for today: understand your workflow shape so we can map to per-token economics and recommend hosted vs dedicated vs private. No slide deck, just questions and notes.

[02:05] Sam Rivera: First question — what does a typical user session look like? Average prompt length, do you keep context, that kind of thing.
[02:20] Renee Martinez: Typical session is 3-6 turns, each turn around 60-120 tokens in user input, responses around 80-200 tokens. We keep full context up to 4 turns, and sometimes attach a 1–2 paragraph knowledge snippet per request. So effective sequence length can spike to 3k tokens when there's long history plus knowledge.
[03:05] Priya Natarajan: Ok that's helpful — sounds like you have both short and occasional long-context calls. For batching, the short ones are good candidates; the long ones will reduce batching efficiency and increase KV cache pressure.
[03:20] Renee Martinez: When you say KV cache pressure you mean the attention cache — the key/value cache for decoding?
[03:26] Priya Natarajan: Yes, exactly. The K V cache, sometimes transcribed as K V cash in our notes, but it's the same. If you reuse prefixes a lot — e.g., similar system prompt and user history — prefix caching can save tokens on model compute and latency.

[05:00] Liam O'Connor: Our throughput expectations: pilot ~50k tokens/day, but if product takes off we would be 1M tokens/day in 6 months. Budget: initial pilot ~$3k-5k per month. Can Redwood do a hosted pilot within that band?
[05:30] Sam Rivera: Short answer: yes, often. We'll map your workload to per-token costs and show batching and caching levers — hosted can be very cost effective for pilot because you avoid reserved capacity. We'll put together a worked example.
[05:52] Dev Patel: Concern: data residency and encryption — we need KMS integration and audit logs if we move to Dedicated or Private later.
[06:02] Priya Natarajan: We support KMS/HSM integrations on Private deployments and have audit logs and RBAC on Dedicated — we'll share the security whitepaper. For hosted we do encryption at rest and in transit and provide SOC2 docs.

[07:15] Renee Martinez: On the per-token model — how do you handle function-calls or tool embeddings? Some requests call an internal retrieval and append an embedding result, that's an extra cost.
[07:30] Sam Rivera: Good point — we separate generation tokens from embedding costs. If you do retrieval-augmented generation, the embedding calls are billed on their own per-embedding unit. For per-workflow cost, we include both generation token cost and embedding unit cost in the worked example.

[09:10] Priya Natarajan: A few levers to hit your $3k pilot: 1) batching window — a small 30–60ms window can fold multiple requests into a single batch, 2) prefix/KV cache reuse — if you pin system prompt and reuse it, we can avoid recomputing prefix, 3) model variant + quantization — using a slightly smaller quantized variant can drop per-token compute significantly.
[09:45] Liam O'Connor: How much does quantization affect latency and quality? We're sensitive to answer coherence.
[09:55] Priya Natarajan: Quantization (8-bit / 4-bit) can change latency modestly— often faster on some hardware and with less memory pressure — but quality can vary by model. We'll recommend test candidates and run evaluation on your prompts. For latency-sensitive pieces, you can route critical flows to a higher-precision hosted variant and less-critical to quantized ones; Redwood supports routing policies.

[11:40] Renee Martinez: Can you explain how dedicated reserved capacity changes unit economics compared to hosted? We're trying to know at what volume it makes sense to switch.
[11:52] Sam Rivera: Sure — Hosted is pay-as-you-go with per-token unit prices and some dynamic routing. Dedicated has a monthly reserved pool that lowers per-token compute because the GPU cost is amortized, plus predictable latency and capacity. Typical break-even depends on model and batching: for consistent sustained throughput (e.g., >400–500k tokens/day on some model families) Dedicated often becomes more economical. We'll show a curve in the model.

[13:30] Dev Patel: Do you offer burst capacity from hosted into dedicated or vice versa? Our traffic spikes at end of month and during campaigns.
[13:42] Priya Natarajan: Yes, we have burst capacity and automated fallback policies. In Dedicated you can configure burst to hosted or to a lower-cost region; in hosted we have higher-tier capacity for enterprise customers. We'll show what the fallback SLOs look like.

[15:05] Liam O'Connor: I want to make sure our SLA for core flow is sub-200ms token latency, is that realistic?
[15:15] Priya Natarajan: Sub-200ms per token is tight but achievable for short responses on optimized hardware with small batch sizes and prefix caching. Long-context calls (multi-k tokens) will naturally exceed that. We need to understand token distribution; please send percentile distributions (p50/p95/p99 length).

[17:00] Sam Rivera: Let's dig into some numbers — assume your pilot mix: 70% short-turn (~120 tokens total per request), 25% medium (400 tokens), 5% long-context spikes (2–3k tokens). With a 50ms batching window and 8k context model, we typically see effective batching of 2–4x on short turns. That 2–4x is where the per-token compute drop happens.
[17:40] Renee Martinez: That makes sense. What about prefix caching: if we have a static system prompt and retrieval answers that are reused across sessions, can that be cached to reduce compute?
[17:52] Priya Natarajan: Yes — prefix caching stores the KV for common prefixes so decoding starts from cached state. It's most effective when the prefix is identical across requests or has high reuse. If your retrieval adds unique tokens each time, cache hit rate drops.

[19:30] Dev Patel: Any rough numbers you can share now — like per-1k tokens cost hosted vs dedicated? I know it depends but a ballpark helps.
[19:40] Sam Rivera: Ballpark— hosted per-1k generation tokens on mainstream open models can be in the low tens of cents with batching and caching; Dedicated per-1k can go down materially depending on reserved commitment. But we'll give you concrete numbers mapped to the exact model family after we see prompts and target SLOs.

[21:10] Liam O'Connor: We're also evaluating privacy needs — if we go Private (VPC/on-prem), what are the main cost deltas?
[21:20] Priya Natarajan: Private typically has higher fixed platform fees (license + support) and infra OPEX you manage. But you get full control over KMS, network isolation, and data residency. Per-token compute cost depends on your hardware; often similar to Dedicated if you provision equivalent GPUs but you add infra management overhead. We can provide an apples-to-apples TCO worksheet.

[23:05] Renee Martinez: For embeddings: we do retrieval at scale. How do you price embedding-heavy pipelines? Also caching of embeddings?
[23:20] Sam Rivera: Embeddings are billed per embedding unit; for caching, if you can reuse document embeddings we recommend storing them and only embedding new docs; for per-query, we account embeddings + generation in the workflow cost. We'll show a scenario where embeddings are amortized across queries.

[25:00] Priya Natarajan: A few operational asks from us to make the model: sample prompt set, distribution of token lengths, percentiles, concurrency numbers (qps), expected monthly token volume, and any retention constraints.
[25:15] Dev Patel: I'll produce a CSV with those metrics — peak qps is approximately 45 at the moment, average qps ~7. Peak concurrency during campaigns goes to ~120.

[27:10] Liam O'Connor: On routing/policies — can you do policy-based routing by cost vs latency? For instance, route to slower quantized model if cost budget exceeded, otherwise go to low-latency variant.
[27:22] Priya Natarajan: Absolutely — Redwood supports routing by policy (latency, cost, region, customer tier) and automatic fallback. You can set a budget gate: if monthly spend passes threshold, new requests are routed to cheaper variants.

[29:40] Renee Martinez: Regarding evaluation: if we send 500 prompts can Redwood run an A/B with quantized vs fp16 and report quality deltas?
[29:52] Sam Rivera: Yes, we have an eval harness; we can run A/B and produce quality/regression reports tied to your prompts. We'll include that in the pilot scope.

[32:00] Dev Patel: What about long-term forecasting tools? We need to show finance a runway if adoption grows 10x.
[32:12] Sam Rivera: We'll include scenario modeling in the workbook: multi-scenario (pilot, 3x, 10x growth) with both Hosted and Dedicated TCOs and suggestions for when to migrate.

[34:00] Priya Natarajan: Small gotcha to watch for — if you use many short requests per session (chatty clients), batching efficiency is great but tokenization artifacts (system prompt repeated) can increase prompt tokens. Consider aggregating user turns before calling the model if that fits UX.

[35:40] Liam O'Connor: This is a bit nitty — do you meter per-token after tokenization? How handle detokenization differences across model variants?
[35:52] Sam Rivera: We meter on tokens as reported by the model tokenizer (so yes after tokenization). Different model families have slightly different tokenization; we normalize in the cost calc and show tokens per prompt as measured by the model in the pilot.

[37:30] Renee Martinez: Any advice on model window sizing? We sometimes switch between 8k and 32k contexts for archived conversations.
[37:40] Priya Natarajan: If most requests are short, 8k is cheaper and faster. Reserve 32k for workflows that truly need it; it increases memory footprint and per-token latency. For mixed workloads, you can route long-context calls to nodes optimized for 32k while keeping short ones on 8k. That's one place Dedicated helps because you can specialize pools.

[40:05] Dev Patel: From an infra perspective, what telemetry will we get? Token-level breakdown, latency per route?
[40:15] Priya Natarajan: Redwood Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-route/model dashboards, traces and error samples. We can also stream logs to your SIEM for audit.

[42:00] Liam O'Connor: Ok recapping — key asks: worked cost model for pilot, pilot scope (50k tokens/day sim), A/B eval plan (500 prompts), and security docs.
[42:15] Sam Rivera: Yep. We'll do: 1) cost workbook with hosted vs dedicated vs private scenarios and break-even curves, 2) Priya-run sim and batching latency numbers, 3) security whitepaper and SOC2 + KMS info, 4) we ask for your prompt corpus and traffic CSV.

[44:30] Renee Martinez: Timeline? We want numbers in hand before our internal budget review on Sept 8.
[44:40] Sam Rivera: We'll target sending the cost workbook and pilot plan by Sept 2, and the sim results by Sept 6 so you have time.

[46:00] Dev Patel: Sounds good. I'll share the prompt set and traffic data by Sept 1.
[46:10] Sam Rivera: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites for a pricing walkthrough and schedule a technical deep-dive with Priya next week if needed.
[46:28] Liam O'Connor: Thanks all.
[46:31] Renee Martinez: Thanks.
[46:33] Priya Natarajan: Thanks — talk soon.

End of transcript
